# Enhancing LSTM performance for financial time series forecasting: the differencing approach - Diff-LSTM

# Levent Gul · Ebru Yuksel Haliloglu · Hande Sevgi · Nukhet Dogan · M. Hakan Berument

Received: 20 November 2025 / Accepted: 12 July 2026 / Published online: 11 August 2026 © The Author(s) 2026

Abstract Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks are increasingly preferred over conventional econometric mod­ els for forecasting non-linear time series such as stock market data. This study proposes the “Diff-LSTM” approach, designed to enhance the forecasting capabilities of standard LSTM networks for non-stationary time series such as stock market data. Unlike conventional applications, the Diff-LSTM methodology trains the net­ work on first-differenced – hence, stationary- series from which forecasts for the original series (in levels) are reconstructed by updating with the observed previous value of the level series. In LSTM networks, due to the limitations of activation functions such as sigmoid and tanh, a downward bias can be observed in forecasts of non-stationary series that have a unit root. Therefore, the proposed Diff-LSTM approach mitigates this down­ ward bias, enabling more reliable forecasts. Diff-LSTM models are evaluated for forecasting accuracy across five major U.S. stock market indices using three cross-validation schemes and four performance measures. The current study demonstrates the superiority of the Diff-LSTM model, which outperformed standard LSTM models in 56 of 60 evaluated instances. This suggests that using Diff-LSTM models improves the forecasting performance considerably.

## 1  Introduction

Recent advances in technology have significantly enhanced the capability to systematically store and analyze large amounts of time-series data. Although traditional econometric models—such as Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), Vector Autoregression (VAR), and Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Het­ eroskedasticity (GARCH)—have proven effective for financial time series, they often struggle with complex, non-stationary and non-linear data structures [1, 12]. Consequently, there is a growing need for models capable of adapting to these complex, non-stationary and non-linear characteristics. In this context, the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, with their short- and long-term memory capabilities, very suitable for time series, have become a very popular deep learning alternative to traditional econometric models [23, 53]. Hochreiter and Schmidhuber [23], the LSTM model is a recurrent neural network architecture explicitly designed to capture long-term dependencies in time-series data. This allows it to propagate weights across layers, maintain the stability of the gradient, and learn continuously. LSTM is a common method for predicting financial data like stock prices, cryptocurrencies, commodity prices and exchange rates (see, for example, Kohzadi, [31, 22, 24, 26, 29, 39, 40, 47, 55, 56, 57, 59, 62]). Comprehensive surveys on LSTM and its applications indicate that LSTM has achieved widespread adoption across various domains (see, e.g. Kim and Nam, [30], Yu, [63, 21]).

This study introduces the Diff-LSTM approach to improve LSTM forecasting performance by addressing the output-range limitation of LSTM cell activation functions. A typical LSTM unit consists of sigmoid and hyper­ bolic tangent (tanh) activation functions, which generate outputs within the ranges of (0,1) and (-1,1), respec­ tively. Mathematically, the outputs of these two activation functions asymptotically approach their threshold values but never reach these threshold values. This causes two problems: one is systematic bias towards lower predictions, and the second is the saturation of functions and their reduced sensitivity to large inputs. The adapted Diff-LSTM approach addresses these limitations by modeling the logarithmic difference and adding the previous observation’s value, rather than modeling the logarithm of the series. Therefore, Diff-LSTM models the return predictions, thereby more effectively leveraging the model’s capacity to capture the complex short- and long-term patterns, non-linearity, and volatility characteristic of financial time series data. The main motivation for the pro­ posed Diff-LSTM approach is conceptually rooted in the seminal work of Dickey [13] and Dickey and Fuller [14] on unit root tests. In their unit root test, the persistent downward bias in the autoregressive parameter, consistently found to be less than 1, was addressed. They proposed differencing the time series as a solution. Similarly, our proposed Diff-LSTM suggests differencing the non-stationary input data before feeding it to the LSTM network to eliminate the downward prediction bias and the sensitivity to large data points inherent in LSTM cells. This paper demonstrates that the Diff-LSTM approach achieves superior forecasting performance compared to a stan­ dard LSTM network.

We conducted extensive empirical comparisons between our proposed Diff-LSTM approach and conventional LSTM networks to verify whether our model enhances LSTM forecasting performance. Five major US stock market indices -the NASDAQ Composite, NYSE Composite, Russell 2000, S&P 500, and Wilshire 5000- were employed to test the performance of the proposed approach with various financial market conditions. The models’ performance was evaluated using four forecast accuracy measures: mean absolute error (MAE), mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), mean squared error (MSE), and root mean squared error (RMSE). Our results are also robust with the Diebold–Mariano test statistic. An important aspect of our work was the application of three distinct cross-validation methods to ensure a thorough evaluation of model reliability. The first cross-validation technique was the traditional time-series splitting (TS), which splits the first 90% of observations into the train­ ing set and the last 10% into the test set. The second validation method used was K-fold time series splitting (FTS) with 10 folds. In this case, the data set was divided into 10 equal parts. The data was trained to a certain point and then tested on the next segment in each iteration - thus preserving the chronological order. The last cross-validation method was blocked K-fold time-series splitting (BFTS) with 5 folds, where each fold was used as a test set and the others for training. Both the training and test sets retain the time series data order to prevent information leakage across folds.

The empirical evidence on the standard LSTM and the proposed Diff-LSTM model provided here suggests that first, the Diff-LSTM provides a significant performance improvement, outperforming the standard LSTM in 56 of the 60 total performance metrics calculated, which constitutes a superiority in approximately 93% of all comparisons (the only exception was its marginally lower performance on four metrics specific to the NYSE Composite index under the TS cross-validation). Second, regarding model stability: standard LSTM performance tends to degrade across datasets, whereas the Diff-LSTM approach reports robustness statistics. This also sug­ gests that the Diff-LSTM model is less sensitive to changes in data structure and can perform well even on smaller data partitions.

## 2  The LSTM model

Standard machine learning algorithms (such as Restricted Boltzmann Machine, Deep Convolutional Neural Networks, Convolutional Neural Network, Deep Belief Network, Stacked Auto-Encoder, and Recurrent Neural Network) work successfully in many important application areas such as image and speech recognition, natural language processing, and big data studies (see, for example, [8, 11, 32, 64]). However, these models do not apply to time-series analysis because of the autoregressive dependencies between sequential observations. Therefore, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have been developed to forecast time series data by incorporating memory mechanisms [48, 50, 52]. RNNs face the problems of exploding gradients or vanishing gradients due to their recursive structure and deep layers.

LSTM solves the long-term dependency problem and can be considered as a better RNN architecture with a feedback loop. ## 3  Motivation and proposed forecasting approach

In a classical linear regression model, when the Gauss–Markov assumptions hold, the OLS estimator of the coefficients is the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE). However, as a special case of classical linear regres­ sion, an autoregressive (AR) process does not meet the BLUE condition because lagged values of the dependent variable are also used as predictors [43]. Bias in estimating AR parameters has been extensively studied [6, 38, 42, 49]. The findings of this line of research indicate that AR parameters are biased by serial correlation, and the bias increases as the true value of the AR parameter approaches 1. Also, the AR parameter is consistently under­ estimated. Orcutt and Irwin, [42] first explicitly identified OLS bias in the estimation of the AR parameter. They showed that the bias arises from serial correlation between the lagged values of the dependent variable originates from two sources. Initially, if the actual mean of the series is known, the serial correlations will generally be biased unless the related autocorrelations are 0. Since the serial correlation and the estimated variance are not independent in general, the bias appears to be towards 0. In fact, the mean is often calculated from the sample, which introduces another bias. This secondary source of bias, which persists even with 0 autocorrelation, is consistently negative in an extensive series; specifically, the expectation of the serial correlation computed from the estimated sample mean is invariably algebraically lower than that computed from the known true mean, and further it gets closer to -1. Similarly, Sastry , [49] studied the biasness in OLS estimation of AR parameters. How­ ever, they studied only the second case mentioned in Orcutt and Irwin [42], and the results were similar. Marriott and Pope, [38], Hurwicz [25], Kendall [28], White [58], Pantula and Fuller [44], Yamamoto and Kunitomo [60], Shaman and Stine [51], Le Breton and Pham [33], Sims and Uhlig [54], and Andrews [3] further elaborated this well-documented problem in the literature.

Similar to the misleading bias in unit root tests, one can observe a downward bias in LSTM cells, because of the inherent limitations of the sigmoid and tanh activation functions. A standard LSTM architecture uses three sigmoid and two tanh activation functions. The sigmoid function has an output range of (0, 1) while the tanh function has an output range of (-1, 1). The tanh function can asymptotically approach the limiting values − 1 and 1, but it cannot take these values exactly. The sigmoid function has an upper bound of 1 which is asymptotically reached slower than tanh, resulting in a limited output range. All these features of the sigmoid and tanh functions in the LSTM cell make the activation functions sensitive to small input values, potentially diminishing predictive accuracy for high-frequency data, such as stock prices. ## 4  Data

The stock market indices used to compare forecasting performance are the S&P 500, NYSE Composite, Wilshire 5000, NASDAQ Composite, and Russell 2000, which are the five leading US indices and are frequently used in such studies. The indices are gathered from Yahoo Finance. These indices consist of companies at different sizes, various industries and have diverse volatility patterns. The S&P 500 Index is based on the market capitaliza­ tion of the largest 500 publicly traded companies in the United States. The Russell 2000 Index is based on the market capitalization of the smallest 2000 publicly traded companies in the Russell Index. The Wilshire 5000 is calculated based on the market value of all actively traded US stocks, and the number of stocks it tracks varies depending on the stocks traded. The NASDAQ Composite Index is a market-cap-weighted index of more than 3700 stocks traded on the NASDAQ exchange, mostly in the technology sector. Finally, the NYSE Composite Index is calculated by including the stocks traded on the New York Stock Exchange.

Daily closing values of the indices were used in the analyses. The starting dates of the indices are as follows: S&P 500, 3 January 1928; NYSE Composite, 3 January 1966; Wilshire 5000, 4 January 1989; NASDAQ Com­ posite, 8 February 1971; and Russell 2000, 11 September 1987. While the start dates of the index data vary, the end date of all indices is 3 September 2024.

Given the output range limitations of the sigmoid and tanh functions, which are (0,1) and (-1,1), respectively, it is essential to assess the unit-root characteristics of the variables under consideration. For this reason, the sta­ tionarity of the five indices used in the comparisons is investigated with the Augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) and Phillips–Perron (PP) unit root tests and the Kwiatkowski–Phillips–Schmidt–Shin (KPSS) stationarity test. The test statistics are provided in Table 2.

The null hypotheses of the ADF and PP unit root tests are the presence of a unit root in the series, while the null hypothesis of the KPSS stationarity test is the stationarity of the series. In Table 2, the ADF and PP unit root tests indicate that all the series have a unit root at levels. On the other hand, the series after first differencing does not have the unit root at 1% level of significance. Likewise, the null hypothesis of the KPSS test is rejected for the level series at the 1% significance level, while it cannot be rejected for the differenced series. The test results for all series therefore suggest that the series are integrated of order 1, I(1).

## 5  Modeling framework

In the present study, comparative analyses using three distinct cross-validation methodologies are conducted to compare the forecasting performance of the proposed Diff-LSTM approach relative to that of the LSTM. In the following subsections, the definition of performance criteria, the details of the cross-validation methods and the hyperparameter optimization process for the LSTM models are explained.

Although a single metric suffices for assessing an individual model’s accuracy, using multiple metrics provides a more robust basis for comparison. Consequently, error-based criteria are prioritized, and four distinct metrics with varying sensitivities are applied.

### 5.2  Cross-validation

Cross-validation is a methodology for assessing model performance by partitioning the data into distinct subsets. Recently, it has been widely used in machine learning for hyperparameter tuning, data partitioning, and model comparison. Primarily, cross-validation enhances model accuracy and facilitates selecting the best-performing model. In the present study, cross-validation methods are used to select the model that exhibits the best perfor­ mance in comparisons. For this, the TS, FTS, and BFTS methods, which are frequently used for time series, are used in our analyses. It should be emphasized that, in literature, mostly one and rarely two of these methods are used together for model justifications. However, herein, all three are used together to provide a more comprehen­ sive evaluation of the proposed approach’s performance.

The TS method is commonly employed as a standard dataset partitioning strategy in machine learning models applied to time series data. To address the autoregressive dependency in time series data, the TS method divides the dataset into training and test sets. Generally, the initial larger partition is devoted to training the model, and the remaining smaller partition is used for testing. This approach acknowledges the inherent sequential nature of time series data.

In the FTS method, the current learning set is divided into K disjoint subsets of approximately equal sizes. Here, “folding” refers to the number of resulting subsets. This division is performed by considering the temporal dependency among the data without replacement. The model is applied to the K-1 subsets, which together rep­ resent the training set. Then, the model is applied to the remaining subset, the validation set, and performance is measured. This procedure is repeated until each of the K subsets serves as the validation set. The average of the K performance measurements on the K validation sets is the cross-validated performance.

The FTS procedure can be summarized as follows:

1.	 Split the dataset into K groups, considering the temporal dependency. 2.	 For each unique group:

a.	 Firstly, the training set and test set for the first fold are determined. b.	 In the following folds, the test set of the previous fold is added to the training set, and the time series con­

tinues without interruption until the last fold. c.	 Fit a model on the training set and evaluate it on the test set. d.	 Retain the evaluation score and discard the model.

3.	 Summarize the performance of the model using the sample model evaluation scores.

The question we address here is how to choose a reasonable value of K that achieves a practical balance between bias, variance, and computation time, so that cross‑validation yields a reliable assessment of models’ forecast­ ing performance. These issues have been largely ignored in the literature, particularly with discrete Bayesian networks. Instead, 10-fold (K = 10) is commonly used without any particular test or specific rationale (e.g., [2, 7, 65]). Breiman and Spector, [9] used expected squared error as the classification error for simulated analytic models they tested and found that the sub-model selection criteria greatly affected validation results, with 5-fold cross-validation providing better results. Therefore, it is important to use an optimal K value to meet the low bias, low variance, and high accuracy requirements of the forecasting models.

Third, the BFTS method is applied similar to the FTS method. However, in the BFTS method, the time series is not continued uninterrupted across folds to prevent back leakage. The BFTS procedure divides the dataset into K non-overlapping folds, accounting for temporal dependencies. A training set and a test set are determined for each fold, and K separate models are trained according to the folds. As a result, the forecasting performance criterion for each fold is calculated separately, and the average across folds is used for model evaluation. Non-overlapping folds break the connections between them and prevent back-leakage of information.

For the present study, within the TS cross-validation framework, the initial 90% of the dataset was allocated to the training set and the remaining 10% to the test set. In the FTS and BFTS cross-validations, the K values are selected as 10 and 5, respectively.
